title: Epic: Real behavioral skill eval framework
description:
## Source

Created from HITL review of agents-bf0.8 after the first synthetic custom-command eval vertical slice.

## Problem

The current skill eval framework proves the plumbing for manifests, trace bundles, deterministic grading, and reports, but the custom-command benchmark is synthetic: with_skill emits expected text and without_skill emits prompts. Pass rates, timing, and usage are schema smoke signals rather than trustworthy behavioral measurements.

## Goal

Move the framework from synthetic/static testing to proper behavior testing by running real agent harness executions, grading generated artifacts with structured deterministic checks, capturing real traces/usage, and promoting observed failures into regression suites.

## Definition of done

- Static harness remains available only for smoke tests and is clearly labeled.
- A real workflow harness can run custom-command cases with and without the skill.
- Reports make it clear whether metrics are synthetic or real.
- custom-command grading checks generated command content and compatibility contracts, not literal expectation prose.
- Real failures can be promoted into regression cases.
close_reason: Completed real behavioral skill eval framework epic with TDD: real Pi harness adapter, real custom-command workflow configs, structured grading, trace/artifact evidence, metric caveats, regression promotion helper, and workflow documentation all validated.

title: Define real harness contract and static-harness boundaries
description:

- [ ] Static harness outputs are labeled synthetic in summary, benchmark, report, and trace metadata.
- [ ] Runner configuration can reject synthetic harnesses for benchmark-quality runs.
- [ ] Tests cover synthetic labeling and real-harness-required validation.

## Notes

Start here so later tasks do not accidentally treat synthetic pass rates as behavioral quality signals.

title: Implement real Pi workflow harness adapter
description:
## What to build

Add a real workflow harness adapter that invokes Pi non-interactively in an isolated sandbox and returns generated response text plus raw session/process artifacts.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Harness can execute one eval prompt through `pi --print` or equivalent non-interactive mode.
- [ ] Harness supports with_skill by force-loading the target skill.
- [ ] Harness supports without_skill by disabling skill loading or omitting the target skill.
- [ ] Raw stdout/stderr, exit status, session metadata, timing, and configured model/provider are captured.
- [ ] Tests use a fake Pi executable or adapter seam so CI does not require API keys.

## Notes

Keep external network/model execution behind explicit configuration; unit tests should validate adapter behavior without calling a live LLM.

title: PRD: Local Pi extended commands
description:
## Problem Statement

The user wants to standardize their command workflow exclusively around Pi while reducing reliance on a broad third-party prompt-template extension. Their existing command library should become Pi-native, predictable, and locally controlled, without losing the convenience of slash commands that select appropriate model, thinking level, and skill context.

The current setup relies on native Pi prompt loading through a prompt-directory symlink and contains some legacy cross-agent command syntax. This creates ambiguity around command ownership, validation, and Pi-specific behavior.

## Solution

Provide a local minimal Pi extension that owns the user’s global command library and registers those commands directly in Pi. Commands remain Markdown files with strict scalar frontmatter. Routing fields let a command optionally choose a model, thinking level, restore behavior, and one skill to inject before execution.

Provide a separate static validation tool for command hygiene. Runtime remains migration-friendly and permissive, while the validator enforces strict Pi-only quality for commands the user chooses to validate.

## User Stories

1. As a Pi user, I want my command library to be registered by a local extension, so that I can control command behavior without relying on a remote package.
2. As a Pi user, I want every command file in my command library to appear as a slash command, so that existing workflows continue to work during migration.
3. As a Pi user, I want commands to optionally declare a model, so that each workflow can run on the most appropriate model.
4. As a Pi user, I want commands to optionally declare a thinking level, so that high-effort workflows can opt into deeper reasoning and lightweight workflows can avoid it.
5. As a Pi user, I want command-triggered model and thinking changes to restore by default, so that one command does not accidentally change the rest of my session.
6. As a Pi user, I want `restore: false` for explicit sticky mode switches, so that I can intentionally change the ongoing session state.
7. As a Pi user, I want commands to optionally declare one skill, so that important workflow expertise is loaded immediately rather than left to model discretion.
8. As a Pi user, I want missing declared skills to fail loudly, so that commands do not silently run without required context.
9. As a Pi user, I want loaded skill content to be visible in the session, so that command behavior is auditable.
10. As a Pi user, I want simple argument placeholders to work in command bodies, so that command files can reuse user-provided input.
11. As a Pi user, I want unsupported legacy command syntax to be surfaced, so that I can clean up stale cross-agent patterns.
12. As a Pi user, I want runtime command execution to remain permissive during migration, so that existing workflows do not break all at once.
13. As a Pi user, I want a strict command validation tool, so that I can deliberately certify individual commands as clean Pi-only commands.
14. As a Pi user, I want the validator to accept command names rather than arbitrary paths, so that validation aligns with slash-command usage.
15. As a Pi user, I want friendly validator output by default, so that command cleanup is easy during editing.
16. As an automation user, I want validator JSON output, so that future scripts can consume validation results.
17. As a maintainer of my agent configuration, I want command filenames to follow a consistent style, so that autocomplete and command discovery stay predictable.
18. As a maintainer of my Pi setup, I want native Pi prompt loading separated from extension-owned commands, so that commands are not registered twice.

## Implementation Decisions

- Build a local Pi extension that owns the global command library.
- The extension registers direct Markdown command files as slash commands.
- Command names are derived from direct Markdown filename stems.
- Command filenames must be lowercase kebab-case and must not use reserved Pi command names.
- V1 is global-only; project-local command ownership is deferred.
- V1 supports only `description`, `argument-hint`, `model`, `thinking`, `skill`, and `restore` frontmatter.
- Runtime warns on unknown frontmatter but still runs commands.
- Clean validated commands require scalar frontmatter with a non-empty `description`; `argument-hint` is optional.
- Frontmatter parsing is intentionally strict and scalar-only.
- Runtime argument substitution supports `$ARGUMENTS`, `$@`, and simple positional placeholders.
- Runtime model resolution supports exact provider/model references and unique bare model IDs only.
- Runtime injects one declared skill as a visible separate context message.
- Runtime fails commands with missing or unreadable declared skills.
- Runtime restores model and thinking after command completion by default.
- `restore: false` explicitly opts into sticky model/thinking changes.
- Runtime does not implement legacy shell/file/body expansion from other agents.
- Runtime excludes loops, chains, deterministic shell execution, subagents, worktrees, parallel execution, and agent-callable prompt execution.
- Add a separate deterministic `command_valid` tool for strict command hygiene.
- `command_valid` validates one command name per invocation only.
- `command_valid` is static only and does not query Pi’s live model registry.
- `command_valid` prints friendly output by default and compact JSON with an explicit flag.
- `command_valid` fails unknown frontmatter, unsupported body syntax, unsupported placeholders, invalid scalar fields, missing descriptions, invalid filenames, reserved names, and missing declared skills.
- Runtime remains more permissive than `command_valid` to support migration.
- Pi’s native prompt directory should no longer point at the command library.
- The extension source remains in the user’s agent configuration repository and is loaded into Pi through a discovery symlink.

## Testing Decisions

- Tests should verify external behavior and command contracts, not implementation details.
- The strict frontmatter parser should be tested with valid scalar frontmatter, malformed frontmatter, nested/list syntax, quoted values, booleans, and empty values.
- Argument substitution should be tested for full raw arguments, joined parsed arguments, positional placeholders, missing positions, and unsupported slicing.
- Command-name validation should be tested for valid kebab-case names, invalid casing, underscores, reserved names, and unresolved command names.
- `command_valid` should be tested as the main deterministic contract.
- `command_valid` tests should cover friendly output, JSON output, exit codes, unknown fields, unsupported legacy syntax, missing descriptions, invalid thinking/restore values, and missing skills.
- Runtime extension behavior should receive a manual Pi smoke test for command registration, model/thinking switching, skill injection, and restore behavior.
- No live model or Pi integration test suite is required for V1 unless explicitly requested later.

## Out of Scope

- Installing or using the third-party prompt-template extension.
- Clean-room parity with the third-party extension.
- Project-local command support.
- Recursive command directories.
- Explicit `name:` frontmatter.
- Nested YAML/list frontmatter.
- Model fallback lists or provider-priority routing.
- Multiple skills per command.
- Deterministic shell/script execution.
- Loops, chains, parallel execution, worktrees, subagents, compare workflows, or boomerang workflows.
- An agent-callable command execution tool.
- Emulating legacy OpenCode shell/file expansion.
- Live Pi/model validation in `command_valid`.
- Whole-library validation mode in `command_valid`.

## Further Notes

The design intentionally separates runtime permissiveness from validation strictness. Runtime prioritizes continuity during migration. The validator defines what “clean Pi-only command” means.

title: PRD: skill_valid validation tool
description:
## Problem Statement

Skill authors need a single trustworthy way to decide whether a repo-local skill is ready to rely on. Today, skill quality is spread across a prose validate-skills checklist, optional behavior eval manifests, live Pi eval runs, and informal maintenance context. This makes it easy for a skill to look complete while missing runnable evals, failing under live Pi, or lacking enough context for future agents to maintain it safely.

## Solution

Provide a Python validation tool named `skill_valid` that validates one repo-local skill at a time through a fail-fast sequence of gates. The tool first performs cheap deterministic checks for target shape, eval manifest structure, and skill maintenance documentation. It then runs a live Pi validate-skills review using the existing validate-skills skill through a wrapper prompt with a strict machine-readable sentinel result. Finally, it runs required live skill behavior evals through the existing skill eval framework, using only the with-skill configuration. The tool prints one compact gate-level JSON result to stdout, exits successfully only for fully valid skills, deletes successful temporary artifacts, and preserves failure artifacts only when needed for debugging.

## User Stories

1. As a skill author, I want one command that validates a skill, so that I know whether it is ready to use.
2. As a skill author, I want validation to fail before live model calls when cheap requirements are missing, so that I do not waste time or model cost.
3. As a skill author, I want the existing validate-skills skill to remain the authoritative spec/best-practice reviewer, so that validation stays aligned with current skill review guidance.
4. As a skill author, I want validate-skills output to be machine-readable, so that CI can fail reliably instead of scraping prose.
5. As a skill author, I want the validation tool to require runnable behavior evals, so that every valid skill has executable evidence of its core behavior.
6. As a skill author, I want live evals to run with the target skill loaded, so that validation proves the skill works under real Pi execution.
7. As a skill author, I want prior regressions to be checked when a regression suite exists, so that known-fixed failures do not silently return.
8. As a skill author, I want unsupported eval suite types to be ignored for pass/fail, so that represented future suites do not block current validation.
9. As a CI maintainer, I want a compact JSON process result and reliable exit code, so that automation can consume validation outcomes without persisted reports.
10. As a CI maintainer, I want explicit live-run opt-in, so that validation never accidentally spends live model calls.
11. As a CI maintainer, I want provider/model/thinking overrides, so that validation can be pinned to a specific execution profile when needed.
12. As a future agent modifying a skill, I want every valid skill to have maintenance documentation, so that I can understand how the skill works and how to update its evals.
13. As a future agent debugging a failure, I want failed live-run artifacts preserved, so that I can inspect what happened without immediately rerunning expensive validation.
14. As a maintainer, I want successful validation artifacts deleted, so that routine validation does not accumulate stale evidence or reports.

## Implementation Decisions

- Build a Python module tool that validates one skill directory per invocation.
- Limit the first version to repo-local skills in the repository's skills collection, while keeping path handling isolated enough for possible external-skill support later.
- Use a fail-fast gate model with deterministic gates before live gates.
- Do not modify the existing validate-skills skill; add a tool-owned wrapper prompt that instructs the live Pi run to use validate-skills and emit a strict sentinel result.
- Treat the final sentinel JSON from the validate-skills run as the authoritative validate-skills gate result.
- Require the sentinel result to contain top-level status, target, and a non-empty list of check results, and pass only when the top-level status and every check status are passed.
- Run the validate-skills live gate with read-only tools only.
- Require an eval manifest that structurally works with the existing skill eval framework before any live eval runs.
- Require a workflow suite and run a regression suite when present; ignore unsupported suite types for validity.
- Execute only the with-skill configuration for live eval validation.
- Integrate with the skill eval framework in process through its public runner function.
- Require strict real-run success for live evals: every required run must be real, non-synthetic, process-passed, and content-passed.
- Require skill-local maintenance documentation with standard sections and concrete references to the skill implementation and declared eval assets.
- Require live Pi opt-in through either an explicit command option or the existing live-eval environment convention.
- Support optional provider, model, and thinking overrides and apply them consistently to both live validate-skills and live eval runs.
- Print one compact gate-level JSON result to stdout and send progress/logging to stderr.
- Do not persist a skill_valid-owned report or summary. Use temporary child artifacts, delete them on success, and preserve them only on failure.

## Testing Decisions

- Test external behavior and process contracts rather than private implementation details.
- Add deterministic unit tests for target path validation, manifest structural validation, maintenance documentation checks, sentinel parsing, live opt-in enforcement, gate-level JSON shape, fail-fast behavior, and live eval result strictness.
- Mock or substitute live Pi and skill eval runner integration in unit tests; live model calls are not required for the unit suite.
- Keep wrapper prompt and terminology documented so future changes to contracts are visible to agents.
- Existing skill eval framework tests are prior art for manifest loading, runner summaries, real/synthetic result caveats, and trace bundle behavior.

## Out of Scope

- Batch validation of every skill in the repository.
- Validating arbitrary external skill directories.
- Persisting successful skill_valid reports or human-readable summaries.
- Requiring all eval manifest configurations to pass.
- Executing unsupported trigger or capability suites.
- Rewriting or replacing the existing validate-skills skill.
- Implementing new skill eval harness types.
- Creating an HTML or rich browsable report bundle.

## Further Notes

The validation domain terminology is captured in the tool-local ubiquitous language document. The most important naming distinctions are that validate-skills is the existing review skill, skill_valid is the orchestration tool, the sentinel result is the authoritative validate-skills output, and strict real-run success excludes skipped, process-failed, not-graded, and synthetic runs.

title: PRD: Skill Eval Framework Vertical Slice
description:
## Problem Statement

Skill evaluation in this repository is currently useful but fragmented. Some skills have hand-built evals and workspaces, while most skills have none. Existing results are difficult to reproduce, compare, or trust because runners, schemas, traces, grading methods, and benchmark formats vary across experiments.

The user wants skill evals to behave like end-to-end regression tests for agent behavior, not just output snapshots. A good framework should verify whether a skill triggers, whether the agent follows the intended process, whether outputs meet contracts, whether bundled resources are used appropriately, and whether the skill justifies its time/token overhead.

## Solution

Build a central skill evaluation framework with a minimal end-to-end vertical slice using the `custom-command` skill as the first target. The framework will provide shared runner behavior, standardized result schemas, trace capture, deterministic grading, and with/without-skill comparison while keeping skill-specific eval data, fixtures, rubrics, and optional custom checks local to each skill.

The first version will prioritize a working workflow-eval slice over full framework completeness. It will run existing `custom-command` eval cases in isolated sandboxes, capture trace bundles and final responses, grade deterministic output contracts, compare `with_skill` against `without_skill`, and produce durable results that can later support trigger evals, regression suites, LLM judges, and richer fixtures.

## User Stories

1. As a skill maintainer, I want one central runner for skill evals, so that every skill is evaluated consistently.
2. As a skill maintainer, I want each skill to own its own eval datasets and fixtures, so that skill-specific behavior stays close to the skill.
3. As a skill maintainer, I want to run a small golden prompt set, so that I can catch behavior regressions before changing or publishing a skill.
4. As a skill maintainer, I want workflow evals to force-load a skill when appropriate, so that I can test whether the skill helps once loaded.
5. As a skill maintainer, I want trigger evals to be modeled separately from workflow evals, so that I do not confuse instruction-following with natural skill invocation.
6. As a skill maintainer, I want eval runs isolated in clean sandboxes, so that results are not affected by previous runs or dirty workspace state.
7. As a skill maintainer, I want each run to save raw and normalized traces, so that I can inspect agent behavior after the run completes.
8. As a skill maintainer, I want deterministic checks for objective expectations, so that simple failures are graded cheaply and reliably.
9. As a skill maintainer, I want optional custom deterministic graders, so that domain-specific output contracts can be checked precisely.
10. As a skill maintainer, I want LLM judges available only for subjective checks, so that nuanced quality can be assessed without making every eval expensive or flaky.
11. As a skill maintainer, I want to compare `with_skill` against `without_skill`, so that I can see whether a skill justifies its overhead.
12. As a skill maintainer, I want to compare current results against previous versions later, so that regressions are visible during skill edits.
13. As a skill maintainer, I want result metrics for pass rate, time, tokens, errors, and deltas, so that quality and efficiency are evaluated together.
14. As a skill maintainer, I want eval suites separated by purpose, so that capability work and regression safety do not get mixed together.
15. As a skill maintainer, I want existing eval files to be usable during migration, so that current work is not thrown away.
16. As a skill maintainer, I want the first vertical slice to use a deterministic, dependency-light skill, so that framework problems are not hidden behind external service failures.
17. As a skill maintainer, I want every real skill failure to become a future regression eval, so that the eval suite compounds over time.
18. As a skill maintainer, I want result data stored in language-neutral schemas, so that the runner can be rewritten or wrapped later without losing historical compatibility.

## Implementation Decisions

- The framework will use a central repo-level runner rather than per-skill custom runners as the default architecture.
- Skill-specific eval data will remain local to each skill, including datasets, fixtures, rubrics, and optional custom deterministic checks.
- The first implementation will be a minimal vertical slice rather than a complete framework rewrite.
- The first target skill will be `custom-command` because it has existing eval cases, deterministic output contracts, no external service dependency, and useful with/without-skill contrast.
- The canonical framework code will live as repo-level tooling, while the skill-authoring guidance will document or wrap that tooling rather than owning it.
- The framework will distinguish forced workflow evals from real trigger evals.
- The first vertical slice may implement forced workflow mode first, but trigger mode will remain first-class in the schemas and design.
- Each run will save a trace bundle containing raw harness output, normalized events, final response/artifacts, timing/usage, workspace diff where applicable, and grading results.
- Normalized traces may start minimal in the vertical slice, but raw trace data will be preserved so future process graders can extract additional signals without rerunning historical evals.
- Deterministic grading will be layered: generic declarative checks first, with optional skill-local custom checks for domain-specific validation.
- LLM judging will be modeled as an optional fallback for subjective checks, not as the default grading mechanism.
- The first `custom-command` slice can run entirely deterministically if no subjective checks require a judge.
- All eval runs will go through a fixture-aware sandbox interface.
- The first slice will use a trivial empty fixture while preserving the abstraction needed for full fixture-copy support later.
- The comparison model will support arbitrary named configurations.
- The first vertical slice will compare `with_skill` against `without_skill`.
- Eval datasets will be organized through a suite-aware manifest.
- Existing eval data can initially be mapped as a workflow suite to avoid unnecessary migration friction.
- Future suites will include trigger, negative, capability, and regression cases.
- The first implementation will be in Python to reuse existing repo eval infrastructure quickly.
- Eval cases, traces, grades, and benchmark data will use language-neutral JSON or JSONL schemas so that a future TypeScript runner or wrapper remains possible.

## Testing Decisions

- Tests should verify external behavior and stable contracts, not incidental implementation details.
- The manifest loader should be tested for suite resolution, skill metadata handling, and compatibility with existing eval definitions.
- The sandbox manager should be tested for isolated workspaces and repeatable empty-fixture behavior.
- The runner should be tested for named configuration execution and correct result organization.
- The trace capture layer should be tested for producing the expected trace bundle shape, including raw output, normalized events, response artifacts, timing/usage, and grading output.
- The deterministic grader should be tested with generic checks such as required content, forbidden content, regex checks, and structured output checks.
- Skill-local custom grading should be supported by interface-level tests, even if the first slice uses only simple custom logic.
- The comparison layer should be tested for pass-rate delta, timing delta, token delta, and per-case result aggregation.
- The first end-to-end test should run the `custom-command` workflow suite through both `with_skill` and `without_skill` configurations and produce comparable results.
- LLM judge support should be represented in schemas and control flow, but not required for the first deterministic `custom-command` slice.
- Trigger eval execution should be deferred if necessary, but trigger suite representation should be covered by schema or loader tests.

## Out of Scope

- Full multi-harness support across every supported agent environment in the first vertical slice.
- Full fixture-copy and repository-reset support beyond the initial fixture-aware empty sandbox.
- Comprehensive trigger eval execution for every skill.

title: PRD: Static optimized-state smell test
description:
## Problem Statement

Users need a fast, deterministic way to check whether a prompt, skill, command, or technical Markdown file appears to be in an LLM-optimized state. Today, optimization relies on manual review and LLM judgment. That makes it harder for programmatic callers to detect obvious token-cost and execution-reliability issues before or after rewrite work.

## Solution

Provide a static smell-test utility for the LLM optimization workflow. The utility analyzes text without any LLM calls, uses exact token metrics through the existing token-counting mechanism, and returns JSON-only output suitable for programmatic callers.

The smell test is intentionally heuristic. It should identify likely issues, not prove correctness. It should help callers and future agents identify optimization candidates while preserving the existing requirement that actual rewrites still need semantic review and confirmation.

## User Stories

1. As a programmatic caller, I want to run a static smell test on a file, so that I can detect likely optimization issues without invoking an LLM.
2. As a rewrite agent, I want categorized findings for token-cost and reliability smells, so that I can prioritize rewrite opportunities.
3. As a caller, I want exact token metrics included in the report, so that optimization state is grounded in the same token-counting approach used by the rewrite workflow.
4. As a caller, I want JSON-only output, so that I can parse results reliably without scraping human-readable text.
5. As a caller, I want stable rule identifiers and finding fields, so that I can filter, aggregate, or display specific smells.
6. As a caller, I want completed analyses to exit successfully even when smells are found, so that subprocess failures mean runtime or usage errors rather than “the file has findings.”
7. As a rewrite agent, I want leading YAML frontmatter excluded from Markdown command/prompt analysis, so that metadata does not create false optimization findings.
8. As a rewrite agent, I want Markdown body content, including fenced blocks, analyzed by default, so that prompt examples and embedded instructions are still visible to the checker.
9. As a maintainer, I want a simple score and pass/warn/fail status, so that callers can make coarse decisions without interpreting every rule.
10. As a maintainer, I want high-signal findings to affect the score and noisier heuristics to remain informational or experimental, so that the tool is useful without becoming overly brittle.
11. As a rewrite agent, I want findings to include suggestions but not automatic patches, so that static analysis does not imply semantic-preserving rewrites.
12. As a skill maintainer, I want the skill instructions to mention the smell test as an optional candidate-discovery aid, so that future agents know when and how to use it.

## Implementation Decisions

- Build a Python static-analysis script as part of the existing LLM optimization skill tooling.
- The analyzer must perform static analysis only and must not call an LLM.
- The analyzer should be heuristic and does not need perfect accuracy.
- The checker should be hybrid:
  - General enough for Markdown, prompt, command, and technical prose.
  - Able to apply extra checks when a file appears to be skill-like or command-like.
- Token metrics should use the existing static token-counting path because token counting does not involve LLM analysis.
- Output must be JSON only.
- Top-level JSON should include:
  - `status`
  - `score`
  - `metrics`
  - `findings`
- Findings should include stable rule IDs, severity, category, location, evidence, message, and suggestion.
- Completed analysis should exit with code `0` regardless of `pass`, `warn`, or `fail`.
- Nonzero exit codes should be reserved for usage or runtime failures.
- Leading YAML frontmatter should be excluded from analysis and token metrics by default.
- The remaining Markdown body should be analyzed by default, including fenced blocks.
- Findings should cover both token-cost and LLM-reliability smells.
- The overall score should start at `100` and subtract fixed penalties by severity.
- Status should be derived from score thresholds.
- Raw metrics and findings should remain available so callers can implement custom gating.
- V1 should score a high-signal core rule set.
- V1 may include weaker or noisier rules as low-penalty informational or experimental findings.
- Findings should include suggestions only, not machine-applicable replacements or patches.
- The rewrite skill instructions should describe the smell test as optional candidate discovery, not a mandatory gate or replacement for semantic verification.

## Testing Decisions

- Tests should validate external behavior rather than internal implementation details.
- The analyzer should be tested through its command-line behavior and JSON output.
- The scoring model should be tested with representative inputs that trigger known severities.
- The frontmatter-exclusion behavior should be tested with Markdown containing leading metadata.
- Token metrics should be tested to confirm the analyzer uses the existing exact token-counting path.
- Rule behavior should be tested with small representative documents rather than exhaustive linguistic cases.
- Skill-like or command-like detection should be tested with representative metadata and body structures.
- The skill documentation update should be verified by inspection or a lightweight text assertion if the repository has a suitable test pattern.

## Out of Scope

- LLM-based judgment of whether a file is optimized.
- Automatic rewriting.
- Machine-applicable replacements, offsets, or patches.
- Human-readable output mode.
- CI-specific fail-on-warning behavior.
- Perfect semantic preservation guarantees from static analysis.
- Exhaustive natural-language linting.
- Mandatory use of the smell test in every rewrite workflow.

## Further Notes

The smell test should be treated as a candidate-discovery and quality-signal tool. It can help identify files that are probably not optimized, but it should not replace the rewrite skill’s semantic-preservation rules, token-count verification for proposed edits, or user confirmation before changes.

Output: JSON-only {status, score, metrics, findings}; success exits 0 for pass/warn/fail; usage/runtime errors nonzero. Metrics use existing count_tokens.py exact static token path and exclude leading YAML frontmatter. Rules: TC001-TC006 token-cost smells; REL001-REL004 reliability/skill-aware heuristic smells. Skill docs updated with optional candidate-discovery guidance. Tests: tools/skill_eval/tests/test_llm_optimized_smell_test.py; validation: python -m unittest discover -v (43 tests OK).

The user wants the repo to become a Pi-specific, downstream-owned resource set where every skill and prompt is maintained for Pi execution quality.

## Solution

Migrate the repository to a Pi-only resource model. Skills, prompt templates, system fragments, validation tools, evals, and maintenance docs will be rewritten or adjusted for Pi’s conventions. Upstream compatibility and OpenCode/Claude portability will no longer constrain design. Existing imported skills remain usable only after being adapted as self-maintained Pi-native resources.

## User Stories

1. As a Pi user, I want this repository to declare Pi as its only target, so that agents do not preserve obsolete cross-agent constraints.
2. As a Pi user, I want prompt templates to use Pi’s supported locations and argument syntax, so that slash commands work naturally in Pi.
3. As a Pi user, I want OpenCode-specific command metadata and expansion syntax removed, so that prompt templates behave predictably in Pi.
4. As a skill maintainer, I want all skills treated as downstream-owned, so that I can optimize them for Pi without worrying about upstream update compatibility.
5. As a skill maintainer, I want imported skills rewritten where needed for Pi, so that their instructions, frontmatter, tooling, and evals match this repo’s runtime.
6. As a skill author, I want skill-creation workflows to use Pi and repo-local eval tooling, so that new skills are created and optimized in the target harness.
7. As a user looking for extensions, I want skill/package discovery guidance to use Pi package mechanisms, so that installation instructions match my environment.
8. As a maintainer, I want validation checks to enforce Pi compatibility, so that broken or non-Pi-native skill metadata is caught early.
9. As a maintainer, I want evals and tests updated away from OpenCode/Claude assumptions, so that validation proves Pi behavior instead of portability.
10. As a future agent, I want repo docs and skill-local maintenance notes to use one consistent Pi vocabulary, so that changes are not pulled back toward cross-agent compatibility.

## Implementation Decisions

- The repository will use Pi as the only supported harness target.
- Prompt templates will be exposed through Pi-supported discovery or package manifest configuration.
- System-prompt append content will be separated from normal prompt templates.
- OpenCode command fields and shell/file expansion syntax will be removed or rewritten as explicit Pi-agent instructions.
- The custom command skill will become a Pi prompt-template authoring skill.
- Pi-native argument features will be allowed and documented.
- Imported/upstream skills will be treated as local downstream forks.
- Claude-centric skill creation, trigger testing, and description optimization flows will be replaced with Pi or repo-local tooling.
- Skill/package discovery guidance will prefer Pi package sources and `pi install`.
- Skill validation will target Pi’s skill behavior and frontmatter support.
- Eval cases and graders will be rewritten to check Pi-native behavior.
- Legal license/attribution files from imported material should remain where required, but upstream update compatibility is not a design constraint.

## Testing Decisions

- Good tests should verify external behavior and resource contracts, not implementation details.
- Prompt-template tests should verify Pi frontmatter, command naming, argument expansion choices, and absence of legacy OpenCode syntax.
- Skill validation tests should verify accepted Pi skill metadata and rejected obsolete assumptions.
- Skill-eval tests should cover rewritten Pi-native skill workflows.
- Rewritten high-impact skills should receive deterministic eval coverage first.
- Live Pi evals should remain opt-in and only run with explicit approval.
- Existing deterministic unit tests should be updated alongside public CLI/API or validation-contract changes.

## Out of Scope

- Maintaining OpenCode compatibility.
- Maintaining Claude Code or Claude.ai workflow compatibility.
- Preserving the ability to update imported skills from upstream without merge work.
- Creating GitHub tracker entries unless explicitly requested.
- Running live Pi/model-backed evals without approval.

## Further Notes

The migration should be staged so the repo contract changes first, then prompt-template/resource discovery, then skill rewrites, then validation/eval updates. The custom-command skill and skill-creator skill are the largest behavior changes and should be handled as explicit workstreams.

title: PRD: macOS Local Pi Diff Review Extension
description:
## Problem Statement

The user wants a focused, macOS-only Pi extension for reviewing local working-tree changes in a native window and converting review feedback into a safe, actionable Pi prompt.

The existing inspiration proves the concept but is too broad and rough: it supports multiple OSes, CDN-loaded assets, extra scopes, and implementation shortcuts. The user wants a clean local extension optimized for their macOS workflow, with reliable local assets, strong git/change modeling, precise comments, and a safe handoff back into Pi.

## Solution

Build a user-local Pi extension that registers one `/diff-review` command. The command opens a native macOS review window showing current working-tree changes only, using a read-only side-by-side Monaco diff view.

The review window lets the user:

- Navigate changed reviewable files.
- See staged/unstaged/untracked and status badges.
- Review regular text files only.
- Comment on original-side or modified-side line/ranges.
- Add file-level and overall feedback.
- Mark files reviewed.
- Finish only when feedback exists.
- Confirm before discarding drafts.
- Confirm before finishing with unreviewed files or stale reviewed/commented files.

On finish, the browser sends structured review data to the host extension. The host validates it, derives snippets from cached snapshot contents, composes a structured fix-request prompt, and inserts it into Pi’s editor. The user manually submits the prompt.

## User Stories

1. As a Pi user, I want to run `/diff-review`, so that I can review my current working-tree changes from Pi.

2. As a macOS-only user, I want the extension optimized for macOS only, so that no effort or complexity is spent on Linux or Windows support.

3. As a reviewer, I want a native review window, so that reviewing code feels separate from the terminal but remains integrated with Pi.

4. As a reviewer, I want to see only changed files, so that the review stays focused on actionable working-tree changes.

5. As a reviewer, I want the review to use one combined working-tree diff against the baseline, so that I review what my repository currently looks like.

6. As a reviewer, I want staged, unstaged, and untracked badges, so that I know each file’s git state without switching scopes.

7. As a reviewer, I want non-ignored untracked files included, so that new files are reviewed before they are committed.

8. As a reviewer, I want ignored files excluded, so that build outputs, caches, secrets, and generated artifacts do not clutter review.

9. As a reviewer, I want renamed files shown as one logical changed file, so that rename context is preserved.

10. As a reviewer, I want deleted text files reviewable on the original side, so that I can comment precisely on removed code.

11. As a reviewer, I want added and untracked text files reviewable on the modified side, so that I can comment precisely on new code.

12. As a reviewer, I want binary, large, symlink, submodule, directory, and unusual-mode paths handled safely, so that the tool never opens unsafe or misleading content.

13. As a reviewer, I want unsupported changed files to be visible as disabled entries when a review window opens, so that omissions are transparent.

14. As a Pi user, I want `/diff-review` to stop with a clear message when no files are reviewable, so that I do not get a dead-end review window.

15. As a Pi user, I want `/diff-review` to stop with a clear message outside git repositories, so that command preconditions are obvious.

16. As a Pi user, I want `/diff-review` to stop with a clear message when there are no working-tree changes, so that no empty review session opens.

17. As a reviewer, I want a collapsible directory tree with fuzzy search, so that I can navigate changed files in project shape.

18. As a reviewer, I want a read-only side-by-side diff, so that original and modified feedback stays visually clear.

19. As a reviewer, I want to click a gutter line to add an inline comment, so that single-line feedback is quick.

20. As a reviewer, I want active same-side selections to create range comments, so that multi-line feedback is precise.

21. As a reviewer, I want inline comments rendered and editable in place, so that feedback stays attached to code.

22. As a reviewer, I want file-level comments, so that I can give feedback about a whole file.

23. As a reviewer, I want an overall note, so that I can give review-wide instructions.

24. As a reviewer, I want reviewed toggles and progress counts, so that I can track review coverage.

25. As a reviewer, I want a warning before finishing with unreviewed files, so that incomplete reviews are intentional.

26. As a reviewer, I want finish disabled until feedback exists, so that the review does not produce empty prompts.

27. As a reviewer, I want a final summary confirmation, so that I can verify comment counts and warnings before sending feedback to Pi.

28. As a reviewer, I want a warning before discarding draft feedback, so that accidental closes or cancels do not lose work silently.

29. As a reviewer, I want the review based on a stable snapshot, so that comments refer to the content I saw.

30. As a reviewer, I want a stale-snapshot warning when reviewed/commented files changed during review, so that I do not submit misleading feedback accidentally.

31. As a keyboard-heavy reviewer, I want minimal review-level shortcuts, so that navigating files and review actions are efficient without conflicting with Monaco typing.

32. As a Pi user, I want Pi’s terminal UI to show a waiting panel while the native window is open, so that I know the command is modal.

33. As a Pi user, I want Escape in Pi to cancel and close the review, so that I can recover if the native window is hidden or unwanted.

34. As a Pi user, I want only one active review session, so that multiple windows cannot race to insert prompts.

35. As a Pi user, I want the generated prompt inserted into the editor instead of sent immediately, so that I can inspect or edit it before Pi acts.

36. As a Pi user, I want confirmation before replacing non-empty editor text, so that existing drafts are not lost.

37. As a Pi user, I want the generated prompt grouped by file, so that Pi can address feedback file-by-file.

38. As a Pi user, I want inline prompt locations to include side-specific line numbers, so that deleted and added-line feedback stays precise.

39. As a Pi user, I want inline snippets included for commented ranges, so that Pi understands the exact reviewed content.

40. As a Pi user, I want snippets derived by the host from cached snapshot content, so that prompt content is authoritative and snapshot-consistent.

41. As a Pi user, I want the prompt to instruct Pi to inspect before editing, preserve unrelated code, run relevant checks when practical, and report skipped/unresolved items, so that fixes are safer.

42. As a local developer, I want all assets bundled locally, so that the review window works offline and does not depend on CDNs.

43. As a local developer, I want a strict local-only content policy, so that accidental external asset/network dependencies are blocked.

44. As a local developer, I want Bun-first install/build/test workflows, so that the extension matches my normal local tooling.

45. As a local developer, I want Pi to load host TypeScript directly, so that extension reloads stay simple.

46. As a maintainer, I want host logic split into testable modules, so that git modeling, classification, IPC validation, staleness, snippets, and prompt composition are reliable.

47. As a maintainer, I want host-side Bun unit tests, so that edge cases can be changed safely.

48. As a maintainer, I want the Monaco/Glimpse UI manually tested for V1, so that the first release avoids heavy browser automation setup.

## Implementation Decisions

- Product form:
  - User-local Pi extension.
  - Not an installable package.
  - One command: `/diff-review`.
  - No supported command arguments.
  - One active review session at a time.

- Platform:
  - macOS is the only supported runtime.
  - The extension may load elsewhere, but invoking `/diff-review` outside macOS fails immediately with a clear unsupported-platform message.
  - No Linux or Windows support, docs, fallbacks, or tests.

- Runtime behavior:
  - `/diff-review` is modal.
  - Pi shows a waiting panel while the native window is open.
  - Escape from Pi cancels and closes the review.
  - Session shutdown cleans up any active native window.
  - Repeated invocation while a review is open warns and does not open another window.

- Git scope:
  - V1 is working-tree only.
  - V1 is changed-files only.
  - V1 uses one combined working-tree diff against the baseline.
  - V1 does not support last-commit review, arbitrary revision ranges, all-files browsing, context-file add, or separate staged/unstaged scopes.
  - Repositories without a baseline commit review staged and non-ignored untracked files as additions against an empty baseline.
  - Outside git, no changes, or no reviewable files stops before opening the native window with a clear Pi message.

- Git/status modeling:
  - Use porcelain status plus targeted diff metadata for staged/unstaged/untracked badges, rename identity, and file status.
  - Include tracked changes and non-ignored untracked files.
  - Exclude ignored files.
  - Detect renamed files and preserve old/new path metadata.
  - Treat deleted regular text files as reviewable with original-side content and empty modified-side content.
  - Treat added and non-ignored untracked regular text files as reviewable with empty original content and modified-side content.

- File classification:
  - Review regular text files only.
  - Binary files, oversized text files, symlinks, submodules, directories, and unusual file modes are unsupported.
  - Text files are too large when either side exceeds 1 MiB.
  - Unsupported files are disabled entries when a review window has at least one reviewable file.
  - If no changed files are reviewable, the command reports unsupported counts and does not open the native window.
  - Binary detection uses git/content signals and a small NUL-byte sniff, with extension-based shortcuts only as convenience.
  - Do not follow symlinks.
  - Do not open submodule contents.
  - Do not show partial previews.

- Snapshot/content behavior:
  - The review window operates on a snapshot.
  - File contents are loaded through the host.
  - Initial metadata opens quickly.
  - The initial reviewable file is prioritized.
  - Other files lazy-load on selection and are cached.
  - The host caches original/modified snapshot contents.
  - Finish performs a staleness check for reviewed/commented files.
  - Stale reviewed/commented files trigger a warning with an option to continue or cancel/reopen.
  - No live file watching in V1.

- Native window/web UI:
  - Use Glimpse and Monaco.
  - Use side-by-side diff only.
  - Diff panes are read-only.
  - Inline comments use Monaco decorations/view zones.
  - File navigation uses a collapsible directory tree with fuzzy search.
  - Badges show git status, reviewed state, comments, and unsupported reasons.
  - Reviewed state is window-local only.
  - Reviewed-without-feedback files are omitted from the generated Pi prompt.
  - Finish is enabled only when overall, file-level, or inline feedback exists.
  - Finish warns when reviewable files remain unreviewed.
  - Cancel/close warns before discarding existing draft feedback.
  - Final submission shows a compact summary modal.
  - No full prompt preview in the native window.

- Keyboard behavior:
  - Minimal review-level shortcuts only.
  - Single-key shortcuts apply only when not typing.
  - Typing in search, comments, inputs, textareas, or Monaco must not trigger review shortcuts.
  - Include finish and cancel/close shortcuts.
  - Full keyboard-only workflow is out of scope.

- Prompt handoff:
  - The browser collects structured review data only.
  - The browser does not compose final prompt text.
  - The browser does not provide authoritative snippets.
  - The host validates review data, checks staleness, derives snippets from cached contents, composes the prompt, and inserts it into Pi.
  - Insert into Pi editor only; never auto-send to the agent.
  - If the editor is non-empty, confirm before replacing it.
  - If replacement is canceled, leave the editor unchanged and notify.

- Prompt format:
  - Human-readable structured fix-request.
  - Overall note first.
  - Feedback grouped by file in sidebar order.
  - Within each file, file-level comments come before inline comments.
  - Inline comments are ordered by side-specific source line numbers.
  - Modified-side comments use working-tree line numbers.
  - Original-side comments use baseline line numbers.
  - Inline comments include concise host-derived snippets.
  - No full diff hunk dumps.
  - No machine-only JSON output.
  - Include instructions to inspect files before editing, address each comment, preserve unrelated code, run relevant available checks when practical, and report skipped/unresolved items.

- IPC/data trust:
  - Use host-generated opaque file IDs.
  - Browser never controls trusted repo paths.
  - Shared typed discriminated unions define host/window messages.
  - Host validates message type, request IDs, file IDs, comment IDs, side, ranges, reviewability, and required fields.
  - No runtime schema library by default.

- Asset/build strategy:
  - Bun installs dependencies, builds web assets, and runs tests.
  - Pi loads host TypeScript directly.
  - Bun does not bundle host code.
  - Bun explicitly builds browser assets; `/diff-review` does not auto-build.
  - Missing built assets cause a clear command error.
  - Web UI uses vanilla TypeScript and plain local CSS.
  - No Tailwind.
  - No Vite by default.
  - No CSS-in-JS.
  - No CDN.
  - No file URL loading.
  - No runtime HTTP server.
  - Host builds one inlined HTML payload containing local JS/CSS.
  - Inlined HTML enforces strict local-only CSP, allowing only required local/inline/blob/data resources.

- Source organization:
  - Thin Pi command entrypoint.
  - Focused host modules:
    - command/session orchestration
    - git snapshot/model
    - file classification
    - content cache/staleness
    - IPC protocol/validation
    - prompt composition
    - asset/HTML building
  - Shared host/web model and IPC types.
  - Separate Bun-built vanilla web app.

- Implementation milestones:
  1. Host-first vertical slice: command, git data, one reviewable file, Glimpse open, read-only Monaco diff, basic submit, host-composed prompt insertion, initial tests.
  2. Host correctness hardening: git modeling, classification, staleness, validation, and tests.
  3. Full reviewer workflow UI: sidebar/search, inline comments, file/overall comments, reviewed toggles, warnings, final summary, shortcuts.
  4. Prompt/insertion polish: grouping, snippets, instructions, editor overwrite confirmation, prompt tests.
  5. Visual polish/manual QA/local docs: layout, badges, states, window sizing, real-repo scenarios, setup/build/reload/use/troubleshooting docs.

## Testing Decisions

- Tests should assert external behavior and contracts, not internal implementation details.
- Host logic should be extracted into deep modules with small, stable interfaces.
- Use Bun unit tests for host-side logic.
- Monaco/Glimpse native UI is manually tested in V1.

Explicitly tested modules:

- Git snapshot/model:
  - outside repo
  - no changes
  - no baseline commit
  - modified/added/deleted/renamed files
  - staged/unstaged/untracked badges
  - ignored file exclusion
  - unsupported-file counts

- File classification:
  - regular text files
  - binary detection
  - NUL-byte sniffing
  - large-file cutoff
  - symlink/submodule/directory/unusual-mode unsupported reasons

- Content cache and snippets:
  - original/modified snapshot contents
  - side-specific line range validation
  - snippet extraction
  - deleted-file original-side snippets
  - added/untracked modified-side snippets

- Staleness detection:
  - unchanged reviewed/commented files
  - changed reviewed/commented files
  - behavior limited to snapshot semantics, not live watching

- IPC validation:
  - accepted request/submit/cancel messages
  - unknown file IDs
  - invalid sides
  - invalid ranges
  - unsupported file comments
  - malformed request IDs/comment IDs

- Prompt composition:
  - overall note first
  - file grouping in sidebar order
  - file-level before inline comments
  - side-specific line labels
  - host-derived snippets
  - omission of reviewed-without-feedback files
  - validation/check instructions
  - no JSON-only output
  - no full diff dumps

- Command/precondition helpers:
  - macOS guard
  - active-session guard
  - missing built assets
  - empty/non-empty editor insertion decision where practical through pure helpers

Prior art:

- The reference extension demonstrates Pi command registration, Glimpse window lifecycle, waiting UI, lazy file loading, and Monaco-based review interactions.
- Pi extension documentation provides the expected command, UI, session shutdown, and local extension loading patterns.

## Out of Scope

- Linux support.
- Windows support.
- Installable package distribution.
- CDN-loaded assets.
- Runtime web asset builds.
- Vite by default.
- Tailwind.
- CSS-in-JS.
- Host-code bundling.
- File URL asset loading.
- Runtime HTTP asset server.
- Full-repository browsing.
- Context-file add.
- Last-commit review.
- Arbitrary revision/range review.
- Separate staged/unstaged review scopes.
- Ignored-file review.
- Partial previews for unsupported files.
- Full diff hunk dumps in prompts.
- Machine-only JSON prompt output.
- Direct editing inside the review window.
- Auto-sending the generated prompt to Pi.
- Persistent review/comment/reviewed state.
- Live file watching.
- Multiple concurrent review sessions.
- Following symlinks.
- Reviewing submodule contents.
- Full keyboard-only workflow.
- Browser-authored final prompts or snippets.
- Runtime schema-library validation by default.
- UI automation for V1.

## Further Notes

- The extension is intentionally local-first and opinionated for the user’s macOS workflow.
- V1 should optimize correctness and safe handoff over broad feature coverage.
- The native window is a review-data collector; the host extension remains the source of truth for git metadata, file contents, validation, snippets, staleness, and prompt composition.
- Future releases may add explicit context files, ignored-file inclusion, last-commit/range scopes, direct quick fixes, prompt preview, richer keyboard workflows, focus-existing-window behavior, or UI automation.

description:
## Problem Statement

Skill authors need `skill_valid` to report whether a skill is ready for reliable LLM consumption, not only whether the skill has the right files and live behavior evals. The repository already has a deterministic LLM-optimization smell test, but it is skill-local and optional, so serious prompt/readability issues can remain outside the standard validation path. This creates a gap: a skill can pass structural and live behavior checks while its primary `SKILL.md` remains hard for an LLM to parse, expensive to consume, or likely to produce unreliable execution.

## Solution

Promote the existing LLM optimization smell test into a reusable repo-level tool named `llm_optimal_check`, promote token counting into a separate repo-level tool named `llm_token_count`, and add `llm_optimal_check` as a deterministic prerequisite gate in `skill_valid`. The gate analyzes only the target skill's primary skill instructions in v1. A check result of `fail` makes the skill invalid; `warn` is non-blocking but visible; `pass` passes. Existing skill-local scripts remain backward-compatible wrappers around the new shared tools. The friendly skill validation shell wrapper renders the new gate and all findings inline so users can see what to fix without rerunning separate commands.

## User Stories

1. As a skill author, I want skill validation to include LLM-optimization readiness, so that skills that are hard for agents to consume do not look valid.
2. As a skill author, I want severe LLM-optimization issues to fail validation, so that invalid skills are blocked before live model cost is spent.
3. As a skill author, I want warnings to remain visible but non-blocking, so that heuristic improvements do not overconstrain releases.
4. As a skill author, I want the validation output to show exact findings with rule, severity, location, message, and suggestion, so that I can fix issues without running another command.
5. As a CI maintainer, I want a stable `llm_optimal_check` gate key in the `skill_valid` JSON contract, so that automation can consume the result consistently.
6. As a CI maintainer, I want `warn` to be a first-class non-blocking gate status, so that CI can distinguish clean passes from pass-with-warning outcomes.
7. As a tool maintainer, I want the reusable LLM optimization analyzer to live in a repo-level tool package, so that validation infrastructure does not depend on a skill-local script layout.
8. As a tool maintainer, I want token counting to live in its own repo-level tool, so that it can be reused independently of the LLM optimization checker.
9. As an existing user of the rewrite skill, I want `smell_test.py` and `count_tokens.py` to remain compatible, so that existing workflows and tests do not break.
10. As a future agent, I want terminology for the new validation domain captured in the tool directory, so that future changes preserve the intended semantics.
11. As a test maintainer, I want `skill_valid` to call the optimization checker through an injectable in-process API, so that tests can simulate pass, warn, fail, and tool error outcomes deterministically.
12. As a validation user, I want tool errors to fail closed with a clear message, so that missing dependencies or broken checks do not silently weaken validation.

## Implementation Decisions

- Add a standalone repo-level LLM optimization checker named `llm_optimal_check` with a command-line interface and an importable in-process API.
- Add a standalone repo-level token counting tool named `llm_token_count` with a command-line interface and an importable API.
- Keep the existing skill-local smell-test and token-count scripts backward compatible by turning them into wrappers around the repo-level tools.
- Add a `llm_optimal_check` gate to `skill_valid`.
- The v1 `llm_optimal_check` gate analyzes only the target skill's primary `SKILL.md` content.
- Gate order is: `target`, `eval_manifest`, `agents_md`, `llm_optimal_check`, `live_opt_in`, `validate_skills`, `live_eval`.
- Extend gate statuses with `warn`; warnings do not make `valid` false.
- Map optimization check status to gate status as follows: `pass` -> `passed`, `warn` -> `warn`, `fail` -> `failed`.
- If the optimization checker errors, the `llm_optimal_check` gate fails closed with an error message and live gates do not run.
- Embed a compact optimization report in the gate details: checker status, score, useful metrics, and all findings, excluding bulky preview/body fields.
- Update the friendly validation shell wrapper to render `warn` in yellow and to render all optimization findings inline.
- Preserve the existing compact JSON process contract for `skill_valid` and the existing JSON contract for the old smell-test script.
- Save a tool-local ubiquitous language document for the new LLM optimization validation domain.

## Testing Decisions

- Test external behavior and process contracts rather than private implementation details.
- Add unit tests for the standalone token counting CLI/API and backward-compatible token-count wrapper.
- Add unit tests for the standalone LLM optimization checker CLI/API and backward-compatible smell-test wrapper.
- Add `skill_valid` tests for optimization gate pass, warn, fail, and checker-error outcomes using an injectable fake checker.
- Add tests proving deterministic prerequisite accumulation still reports multiple missing requirements and skips live gates when the optimization gate fails.
- Add friendly wrapper tests or deterministic script checks proving `warn` renders yellow/non-blocking and optimization findings render inline.
- Preserve existing smell-test JSON contract tests as prior art.
- Avoid live Pi integration tests for this feature; use fakes/mocks for live gates.

## Out of Scope

- Running the optimization checker on `AGENTS.md`, reference docs, eval manifests, eval prompts, generated reports, or all Markdown assets.
- Making optimization warnings block validity.
- Replacing live validate-skills review with the deterministic optimization checker.
- Adding LLM-based judging to the optimization checker.
- Changing the existing optimization heuristic thresholds unless needed to preserve current behavior after extraction.
- Removing or breaking existing skill-local script entry points.
- Persisting new validation reports outside the existing `skill_valid` stdout JSON and failure artifacts behavior.

## Further Notes

The key naming decision is that `llm_optimal_check` is the reusable optimization-readiness checker and the `skill_valid` gate key, while `llm_token_count` is a separate reusable token-counting tool. The older phrase “smell test” remains only as backward-compatible script wording for existing users. The optimization check is deterministic and heuristic; `fail` is blocking, `warn` is visible but non-blocking, and tool errors fail closed.
close_reason: Implemented PRD: standalone llm_token_count and llm_optimal_check tools, compatibility wrappers, skill_valid llm_optimal_check warn/fail gate, friendly wrapper rendering, docs, and hardening tests. Validated with python3 -m unittest discover -v (48 tests).

## What to build

Create the standalone `llm_token_count` repo tool as the first tracer bullet: expose a CLI and importable API that preserve the exact token metrics currently produced by the legacy token-count script, then turn the legacy skill-local token script into a compatibility wrapper.

- [ ] `python3 -m tools.llm_token_count` accepts stdin and emits the same human/default output contract as the current token-count script.
- [ ] `python3 -m tools.llm_token_count --json` emits the same JSON metric fields as the current token-count script.
- [ ] An importable API returns exact token metrics for caller-provided text.
- [ ] The legacy `count_tokens.py` entry point remains compatible by delegating to the repo-level tool.
- [ ] Existing token-count tests pass or are migrated without changing expected behavior.

## Classification

- Slice type: AFK
- Beads type: task
- Priority: 2

## Blocked by

None — can start immediately.

## Notes for future agents

Preserve exact counting behavior and bootstrap assumptions. This tool is standalone; do not bury token counting inside `llm_optimal_check`.
